public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 307

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/307](https://www.erdosproblems.com/307)
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace Erdos307

open scoped Finset

/--
Are there two finite set of primes $P$ and $Q$ such that

$$
1 = \left( \sum_{p \in P} \frac{1}{p} \right) \left( \sum_{q \in Q} \frac{1}{q} \right)
$$
?

Asked by Barbeau [Ba76].

[Ba76] Barbeau, E. J., _Computer challenge corner: Problem 477: A brute force program._
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_307 : answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ P Q : Finset ℕ, (∀ p ∈ P, p.Prime) ∧ (∀ q ∈ Q, q.Prime) ∧
    1 = (∑ p ∈ P, (p : ℚ)⁻¹) * (∑ q ∈ Q, (q : ℚ)⁻¹) := by
  sorry

/--
Instead of asking for sets of primes, ask only that all elements in the sets be relatively coprime.

Cambie has found several examples when this weakened version is true. For example,
$$
1=\left(1+\frac{1}{5}\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3}\right)
$$
and
$$
1=\left(1+\frac{1}{41}\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{7}\right).
$$
-/
@[category textbook, AMS 5 11]
theorem erdos_307.variants.coprime : answer(True) ↔ ∃ P Q : Finset ℕ, 0 ∉ P ∩ Q ∧ 1 < #P ∧ 1 < #Q ∧
    Set.Pairwise P Nat.Coprime ∧ Set.Pairwise Q Nat.Coprime ∧
    1 = (∑ p ∈ P, (p : ℚ)⁻¹) * (∑ q ∈ Q, (q : ℚ)⁻¹) := by
  show True ↔ _
  simp only [Finset.mem_inter, not_and, true_iff]
  use {1, 5}, {2, 3}
  norm_num +decide

/--
There are no examples known of the weakened coprime version if we insist that $1\not\in P\cup Q$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5 11]
theorem erdos_307.variants.coprime_one_notMem : answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ P Q : Finset ℕ, 0 ∉ P ∩ Q ∧ 1 ∉ P ∪ Q ∧
    1 < #P ∧ 1 < #Q ∧ Set.Pairwise P Nat.Coprime ∧ Set.Pairwise Q Nat.Coprime ∧
    1 = (∑ p ∈ P, (p : ℚ)⁻¹) * (∑ q ∈ Q, (q : ℚ)⁻¹) := by
  sorry

/--
A machine-checked **barrier** for Erdős 307 (Bonfioli, 2026): any solution with `Q` nonempty uses at
least 59 primes in total, and `(∏_{p ∈ P} p)² ≥ 4·10¹¹²` — i.e. `∏_{p ∈ P} p ≥ 2·10⁵⁶` (and, by
symmetry, the same for `∏ Q`); so no solution lies below a prime-product of `2.09·10⁵⁶`. The full
`sorry`-free proof is in the linked repository (`Closed.lean`): the left conjunct is `card_ge_59`,
the right is `erdos307_barrier_closed`. Both depend on `propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound` and
nothing further: the evaluation of the first 59 primes is kernel-checked by `decide`, so no
`native_decide` enters this statement.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at
"https://github.com/ElVec1o/erdos307/blob/76d242b024102f32d8411c714be4ad140a8b7c4b/lean/Erdos307/Closed.lean#L121"]
theorem erdos_307.barrier {P Q : Finset ℕ}
    (hP : ∀ p ∈ P, p.Prime) (hQ : ∀ q ∈ Q, q.Prime) (hQne : Q.Nonempty)
    (heq : 1 = (∑ p ∈ P, (p : ℚ)⁻¹) * (∑ q ∈ Q, (q : ℚ)⁻¹)) :
    59 ≤ #(P ∪ Q) ∧ (4 * 10 ^ 112 : ℚ) ≤ (∏ p ∈ P, (p : ℚ)) ^ 2 := by
  sorry

/--
A stronger machine-checked **barrier** (Bonfioli, 2026), closing the 59-prime level: any solution of
Erdős 307 in fact uses at least `60` primes in total. The full `sorry`-free proof is `erdos307_sixty`
in the linked repository (`Sixty.lean` at tag `v1.1.1`); its only non-logical input is a `native_decide`
depth-first search establishing that no admissible 59-prime support survives the Pythagorean
`plus`-value square test, with axioms `propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound` together with that
`native_decide`.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at
"https://github.com/ElVec1o/erdos307/blob/080164a8db2eeb20f65c362894ec93f12448609a/lean/Erdos307/Sixty.lean#L367"]
theorem erdos_307.barrier_sixty {P Q : Finset ℕ}
    (hP : ∀ p ∈ P, p.Prime) (hQ : ∀ q ∈ Q, q.Prime)
    (heq : 1 = (∑ p ∈ P, (p : ℚ)⁻¹) * (∑ q ∈ Q, (q : ℚ)⁻¹)) :
    60 ≤ #(P ∪ Q) := by
  sorry

end Erdos307

findings.description: The docstring concludes “so no solution lies below a prime-product of `2.09·10⁵⁶`,” but the declaration establishes the rounded bound `(4 * 10^112 : ℚ) ≤ (∏ p ∈ P, (p : ℚ))^2`, equivalent to `∏ P ≥ 2·10⁵⁶`. The sharper constant is a separate paper result, not the conclusion of this machine-checked theorem. The Lean statement itself correctly matches its linked proof.
findings.source_evidence: The pinned Closed.lean explicitly distinguishes the constants: “The paper's `thm:barrier` states the sharp `2.09·10⁵⁶`; what is machine-checked here is the rounded `2·10⁵⁶` ... The sharp value is a paper result, not a Lean one.” See https://github.com/ElVec1o/erdos307/blob/76d242b024102f32d8411c714be4ad140a8b7c4b/lean/Erdos307/Closed.lean, opening documentation.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace `2.09·10⁵⁶` in the concluding sentence with `2·10⁵⁶`, or explicitly distinguish the paper's sharper bound from the rounded bound formalized here.

findings.description: The docstring describes the depth-first search as the pinned proof's only non-logical input. At the cited v1.1.1 commit, however, `native_decide` also proves the prime-count facts `np0` through `np59` and eight auxiliary forced-prime/pool facts. Thus the description of which computations use native evaluation is inaccurate for this reference. The formal proof exists, proves the correct statement, and explicitly permits native evaluation; this is not an invalid proof record or a status issue.
findings.source_evidence: At https://github.com/ElVec1o/erdos307/blob/080164a8db2eeb20f65c362894ec93f12448609a/lean/Erdos307/Sixty.lean, lines 345–361 use `native_decide` for eight auxiliary facts as well as `dfs_run`. At the same commit, lean/Erdos307/Numeral.lean uses `native_decide` for all sixty prime-count facts. Recompilation and `#print axioms Erdos307.erdos307_sixty` confirmed these dependencies.
findings.suggested_fix: Describe the pinned proof as using `native_decide` for the DFS and auxiliary numeral/enumeration checks, rather than for the DFS alone.

reformulations.difference: The theorem uses natural-number denominators and excludes zero only from `P ∩ Q`, rather than directly requiring positive denominators in both sets. Despite appearances, no admissible witness can contain zero.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: If zero belongs to P, pairwise coprimality and `1 < #P` force P = {0,1}, so its reciprocal sum is 1. The intersection condition then excludes zero from Q, and the product equation forces Q's reciprocal sum to equal 1. A sum of reciprocals of positive pairwise-coprime integers has denominator equal to their product in lowest terms; if that sum is an integer, every denominator must be 1. This contradicts `1 < #Q`. The symmetric argument excludes zero from Q. Consequently replacing the intersection by a union changes no candidate. This pointwise equivalence is proved as `Review307.coprime_zero_exclusion_iff` in /workspace/review/scratch.lean. Both source examples also satisfy the explicit nontrivial cardinality conditions.

reformulations.difference: The source asks for the coprime version with positive denominators other than 1. Lean instead uses `Finset ℕ`, excludes 1 from the union and zero from the intersection, and explicitly requires both cardinalities to exceed 1.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Pairwise coprimality makes any element distinct from zero in a set containing zero equal to 1. Excluding 1 and requiring cardinality greater than 1 therefore excludes zero from each set, so all denominators are at least 2. Conversely, for denominators at least 2, the equation rules out empty sets. A singleton on either side would force the other reciprocal sum to be an integer, impossible for a nonempty pairwise-coprime set of denominators at least 2. Thus the cardinality bounds are automatic. The complete pointwise equivalence with the source-style formulation is proved as `Review307.no_one_source_iff` in /workspace/review/scratch.lean.

review.notes: All five formal statements were checked and are faithful to their cited mathematical claims. The source still records the prime problem and the no-1 coprime variant as open. Lean experiments verified both displayed coprime examples, empty-set behavior, the equivalences above, and the absence of solutions among subsets of primes below 20. Both pinned external proof chains were recompiled in workspace scratch files and shown to imply the exact repository statements; neither depends on sorryAx. The first uses only the three standard axioms, while the second additionally uses native evaluation. No repository files were edited.
